concept: Hypoxia - definition: a condition of the body in which the tissues are starved of oxygen
q: What is hypoxia?
a: Hypoxia is a condition of the body in which the tissues are starved of oxygen, so the cells cannot do their work. Oxygen deficiency is the common thread in all four types. Onset is insidious and the early signs include euphoria, impaired judgment, slowed reaction time, tingling, headache, narrowed vision and cyanosis; the pilot usually feels fine while performance is already decaying.
dup: What is hypoxia?

concept: Hypoxic hypoxia - insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole
q: What is hypoxic hypoxia?
a: Hypoxic hypoxia is insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole, and it is the altitude form. As you climb, ambient pressure falls, so the partial pressure of oxygen in the lungs is too low to saturate the blood. A blocked airway, a failed oxygen system or simply cruising unpressurized at high altitude will produce it. The treatment is oxygen and an immediate descent.
dup: What is hypoxic hypoxia and why does it occur at altitude?

concept: Hypemic hypoxia - blood unable to take up and transport sufficient oxygen to the cells
q: What is hypemic hypoxia?
a: Hypemic hypoxia occurs when the blood cannot take up and transport a sufficient amount of oxygen to the cells, even though the air supply is adequate. Causes include anemia, blood loss, a recent blood donation, sickle cell disease and, above all, carbon monoxide, which binds to hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does. Oxygen, descent and removing the cause are the fixes.
dup: What is hypemic hypoxia and what causes it?

concept: Stagnant hypoxia - oxygen-rich blood in the lungs is not moving, so oxygen is not delivered to the tissues
q: What is stagnant hypoxia?
a: Stagnant hypoxia results when the oxygen-rich blood is not moving, so oxygen never reaches the tissues. The lungs load the blood normally but circulation fails or is restricted: low cardiac output, shock, a cramped or crossed limb, cold extremities, or the pooling of blood under sustained positive G in an aggressive maneuver. Restore circulation, keep warm, and descend.
dup: What is stagnant hypoxia?

concept: Histotoxic hypoxia - inability of the cells to effectively use the oxygen delivered to them
q: What is histotoxic hypoxia?
a: Histotoxic hypoxia is the inability of the cells to effectively use oxygen. The air, the blood and the circulation are all working, but the cells themselves are poisoned and cannot metabolize the oxygen delivered. Alcohol, narcotics, cyanide and some other drugs cause it, which is one reason a hangover is so dangerous at altitude. Oxygen alone does not fix it; the substance must clear the body.
dup: What is histotoxic hypoxia?

concept: Hypoxia solution - don an oxygen mask if available and descend immediately to the lowest practical altitude
q: You suspect hypoxia in cruise. What do you do?
a: Don an oxygen mask if one is available and descend immediately to the lowest practical altitude, then land and have the cause found. Use 100 percent oxygen if you have it, reduce workload, ventilate the cabin, and tell ATC or a passenger, because your own judgment is the first faculty hypoxia degrades. If you cannot tell hypoxia from hyperventilation, treat it as hypoxia.
dup: What do you do if you suspect hypoxia in flight?

concept: Hyperventilation - definition: excessive rate and depth of respiration causing abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood
q: What is hyperventilation?
a: Hyperventilation is an excessive rate and depth of respiration leading to an abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood. It is normally brought on by stress, fright, anxiety or pain rather than by any shortage of oxygen. The resulting chemical imbalance produces dizziness, tingling in the fingers and toes, hot and cold sensations, muscle spasm, drowsiness and finally unconsciousness.
dup: What is hyperventilation and what causes it?

concept: Hyperventilation symptoms resemble hypoxia; correct diagnosis matters and when in doubt treat it as hypoxia and get lower
q: Hypoxia and hyperventilation feel alike. How do you sort them out in flight?
a: Often you cannot, so when in doubt, treat it as hypoxia: go on oxygen and get to a lower altitude as soon as possible. Hypoxia is the one that can kill in minutes, and oxygen does no harm to a hyperventilating pilot. The clues are that hyperventilation usually follows stress and is unrelated to altitude, while hypoxia worsens with height; if oxygen brings no relief, slow the breathing instead.
dup: How do you distinguish hypoxia from hyperventilation, and why does it matter?

concept: Hyperventilation solution - slow the breathing and increase carbon dioxide intake by breathing into a bag
q: How do you treat hyperventilation?
a: Slow the rate of breathing and increase carbon dioxide intake by breathing into a bag or into cupped hands so that exhaled air is rebreathed. Talking aloud, singing or counting out loud works too, because it forces a normal breathing rhythm. Symptoms clear within a few minutes as carbon dioxide is restored; if they do not, assume hypoxia and use oxygen and descent.
dup: How do you treat hyperventilation?

concept: Carbon monoxide - a colorless, odorless, tasteless deadly gas from combustion of carbon based materials, usually exhaust entering the cabin
q: What is carbon monoxide and how does it get into the cabin of your Warrior?
a: Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless, tasteless deadly gas produced by the combustion of carbon based materials, and in an airplane it is almost always exhaust gas finding its way into the cabin. The 1981 PA-28-161 draws its cabin heat from a shroud wrapped around the exhaust muffler, so a crack or burned seam in that muffler or heat exchanger lets exhaust pass straight into the heat duct and into the cockpit.
dup: Where does carbon monoxide in a light aircraft cabin come from?

concept: Carbon monoxide symptoms usually start with drowsiness and come on quickly
q: What are the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning and how fast do they come on?
a: They usually start with drowsiness and come on quickly, followed by headache, dizziness, a feeling of sluggishness or warmth, blurred vision, impaired judgment and loss of muscular power, and in severe cases convulsions and unconsciousness. The gas cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, so the first practical warning is often a darkened detector spot or an unexplained headache with the heat on.
dup: What are the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning in flight?

concept: Carbon monoxide solution - turn the cabin heat off, ventilate the cabin, open a window, land as soon as possible
q: You get a headache and drowsiness with the cabin heat on in the Warrior. What do you do?
a: Turn the cabin heat off at once, ventilate the cabin as much as possible by opening the fresh air vents and the storm window, and land as soon as possible. Use supplemental oxygen if it is aboard and stay low, because carbon monoxide produces hypemic hypoxia. Do not fly the airplane again until a mechanic has inspected and pressure checked the muffler and the heat exchanger shroud that feeds the cabin heat.
dup: What do you do if you suspect carbon monoxide in the cabin?

concept: Types of medicals under 61.23 - which class of certificate goes with which privileges
q: What does 61.23 require, and which class of medical goes with which privileges?
a: It requires you to hold the class of medical certificate that matches the privileges you exercise: first class for airline transport pilot, second class for commercial, third class for private, recreational, student and flight instructor privileges. A higher class covers the privileges of a lower one for as long as it remains valid at that level. The rule is 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: What class of medical certificate does a commercial pilot need?

concept: First class medical is required for Airline Transport Pilot privileges
q: Who needs a first class medical certificate?
a: A first class medical is required to exercise airline transport pilot privileges, and while it lasts it also covers commercial and private privileges. It is the strictest standard and is issued by an Aviation Medical Examiner authorized for first class examinations, which is why airline and many corporate pilots hold one. See 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a first class medical valid for airline transport pilot privileges?

concept: First class valid 12 calendar months if the pilot is under age 40, then it reverts to third class privileges
q: How long is a first class medical good for a pilot under 40, and what happens after that?
a: For a pilot under age 40 on the date of the examination it carries airline transport pilot privileges for 12 calendar months. Because second class privileges also run 12 calendar months, nothing is gained at that level, so when the first year lapses it simply continues as a third class medical, which for an under-40 pilot runs to 60 calendar months from the examination. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a first class medical valid for airline transport pilot privileges?

concept: First class valid 6 months if the pilot is 40 or over, then second class privileges for 6 months, then third class privileges
q: A pilot aged 45 holds a first class medical. Walk me through how it steps down.
a: At age 40 or over the first class medical carries airline transport pilot privileges for only 6 calendar months. It then holds second class, commercial privileges for a further 6 months, which is 12 calendar months in total from the examination. After that it serves as a third class medical out to 24 calendar months from the examination, because the holder was 40 or over. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a first class medical valid for commercial pilot privileges?

concept: Second class medical is required for Commercial Pilot privileges and is valid 12 calendar months regardless of age
q: How long is a second class medical valid for commercial privileges?
a: A second class medical is required to exercise commercial pilot privileges and is valid for them for 12 calendar months regardless of the pilot's age. Age makes no difference at this level; it only changes the length of the third class tail that follows. The requirement and the duration are both in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a second class medical valid for commercial pilot privileges?

concept: When the second class period lapses it reverts to third class privileges
q: Your second class medical passes 12 months. What may you still do with it?
a: It reverts to third class privileges, so you may fly as a private, recreational or student pilot or as a flight instructor, but you may no longer fly for compensation or hire. That third class tail lasts to 60 calendar months from the examination if you were under 40 on the examination date, or 24 calendar months if you were 40 or over. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long does a second class medical remain valid for private pilot or flight instructor privileges?

concept: Third class medical is required for Private Pilot, Flight Instructor or Student Pilot
q: Who needs a third class medical certificate?
a: A third class medical is required for private pilot, student pilot and flight instructor privileges, and for recreational pilot privileges. A flight instructor needs one only when acting as pilot in command or as a required flight crewmember, and a sport pilot may use a valid U.S. driver's license instead. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration lists who must hold which class.

concept: Third class valid 60 calendar months (5 years) if the pilot is under age 40
q: How long is a third class medical valid for a pilot under 40?
a: 60 calendar months, that is 5 years, when the pilot was under age 40 on the date of the examination. It runs to the end of the last day of the sixtieth month, so an examination on March 3 is good through March 31 five years later. The figure is in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a third class medical valid?

concept: Third class valid 24 calendar months if the pilot is age 40 or over
q: How long is a third class medical valid for a pilot aged 40 or older?
a: 24 calendar months when the pilot was age 40 or over on the date of the examination, half the under-40 duration. The age that counts is the age at the examination, not the age the pilot happens to be when flying, so turning 40 during the life of the certificate does not shorten it. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.
dup: How long is a third class medical valid?

concept: Medical durations are counted in calendar months and the age used is the pilot's age on the date of the examination
q: What does calendar month mean for a medical, and which age sets the duration?
a: A medical runs in calendar months and expires at the end of the last day of the final month, so an examination on June 12 valid for 12 calendar months is good through June 30 of the following year. The age that fixes the duration is the pilot's age on the date of the examination, which is the classic trap: a pilot who was 39 at the examination keeps the under-40 durations for the whole life of that certificate. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.

concept: BasicMed - an alternate way for pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate if certain requirements are met
q: What is BasicMed?
a: BasicMed is an alternate way for a pilot to fly certain small aircraft without holding an FAA medical certificate, after a physical examination by a state-licensed physician and an online medical education course. It is not a medical certificate. The requirements are in 14 CFR Part 68, Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate, which has no subparts, and the privileges in Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i).
dup: Is BasicMed a medical certificate?

concept: BasicMed eligibility - possess a U.S. driver's license
q: What must you hold in place of a medical certificate to fly under BasicMed?
a: A valid U.S. driver's license, and you must comply with every restriction on it, such as corrective lenses. The license is your day-to-day evidence of fitness under 14 CFR Part 68, Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate, which has no subparts. Carry the license, the course completion certificate and the completed physician checklist whenever you fly under BasicMed.
dup: What are the eligibility requirements to use BasicMed in the first place?

concept: BasicMed eligibility - must have held an FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006
q: What prior FAA medical history do you need before you can use BasicMed?
a: You must have held an FAA medical certificate of any class that was valid at some point after July 14, 2006, and it must not have been revoked, suspended or withdrawn, nor your most recent application for one denied. A pilot who has never held an FAA medical, or whose last application was denied, must see an Aviation Medical Examiner first. 14 CFR Part 68, Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate, which has no subparts.
dup: What are the eligibility requirements to use BasicMed in the first place?

concept: BasicMed eligibility - physical examination by a state-licensed physician using the Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist
q: What examination does BasicMed require, how often, and on what form?
a: A physical examination by any state-licensed physician every 48 calendar months, carried out using the Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist, FAA Form 8700-2, which you and the physician both sign and which you keep. The physician need not be an Aviation Medical Examiner. The rules are 14 CFR Part 68, which has no subparts, section 68.5 Comprehensive medical examination and section 68.7 Comprehensive medical examination checklist.
dup: What must you do, and how often, to operate under BasicMed?

concept: BasicMed eligibility - complete a BasicMed medical education course
q: What course does BasicMed require, and how often must you repeat it?
a: A free online BasicMed medical education course taken every 24 calendar months, covering aeromedical factors and the pilot's duty not to fly when unfit. You keep the completion certificate and make the logbook entry. The requirement is 14 CFR Part 68, which has no subparts, section 68.3 Medical education course requirements. Note the mismatched clocks: 24 months for the course against 48 months for the physical.
dup: What must you do, and how often, to operate under BasicMed?

concept: BasicMed aircraft requirement - any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants
q: How many occupants may a BasicMed aircraft be authorized to carry?
a: Not more than 7 occupants, crew included, as the aircraft is authorized to carry under federal law. This is a limit on the aircraft's certification and is separate from the limit on how many passengers you may actually carry on the flight. It is in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i).

concept: BasicMed aircraft requirement - maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds
q: What is the weight limit on an aircraft flown under BasicMed?
a: A maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds. Transport category rotorcraft certificated under Part 29 are excluded from BasicMed whatever they weigh. The limit is in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i); your PA-28-161 Warrior II sits far inside it.
dup: What are the current aircraft and operating limits for BasicMed?

concept: BasicMed operating requirement - carries not more than 6 passengers
q: How many passengers may you carry on a BasicMed flight?
a: No more than 6 passengers on board, which with one pilot keeps the airplane inside the 7 occupant ceiling. This one is a limit on the operation rather than on the aircraft's certification, so a seven seat airplane flown with six passengers and a single pilot is legal. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i).
dup: What are the current aircraft and operating limits for BasicMed?

concept: BasicMed operating requirement - VFR or IFR, within the United States, at or below 18,000 feet
q: Where, and under what flight rules, may you fly on BasicMed?
a: VFR or IFR, within the United States, at or below 18,000 feet MSL. An instrument rating and instrument currency are still needed to fly IFR, and BasicMed itself puts no restriction on night flight. Flying into another country requires that country's authorization. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i).

concept: BasicMed operating requirement - not exceeding 250 knots
q: Is there a speed limit on a BasicMed flight?
a: Yes. The aircraft may not be operated at an indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots. The speed limit sits alongside the 18,000 foot ceiling and keeps BasicMed to the slower end of general aviation. It is carried in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i).

concept: BasicMed operating requirement - the flight may not be operated for compensation or hire
q: Can you exercise your commercial privileges under BasicMed?
a: No. A BasicMed flight may not be operated for compensation or hire and the pilot may not be paid, so any commercial work requires a second class medical certificate. What BasicMed gives you is essentially private pilot privileges, including the cost sharing exceptions in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E (Private Pilots), section 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, whose paragraph (i) carries the BasicMed conditions.

concept: The leans is the most common illusion in flight
q: Which spatial disorientation illusion is the most common in flight?
a: The leans, by a wide margin, and nearly every instrument pilot meets it sooner or later. It is a vestibular illusion in which the semicircular canals fail to register a slow roll, so the pilot's sense of the vertical ends up tilted while the attitude indicator shows the truth. Believing the instruments rather than the seat of the pants is the only cure.
dup: What causes the leans and what wrong input does it invite?

concept: The leans - caused by a sudden return to level flight following a gradual and prolonged turn that went unnoticed
q: What causes the leans?
a: A sudden return to level flight following a gradual and prolonged turn that went unnoticed by the pilot. The roll into the turn was slower than the threshold the semicircular canals can detect, so the brain accepted the banked attitude as level; the abrupt roll back to wings level is detected, and it feels like a bank in the opposite direction.
dup: What causes the leans and what wrong input does it invite?

concept: The leans - the pilot may lean in the direction of the original turn to regain the perception of correct vertical posture
q: What will a pilot with the leans do, and what is the danger?
a: The pilot may physically lean in the direction of the original turn in a corrective attempt to regain the perception of a correct vertical posture, and may hold a wing down or roll back into the bank so that the picture matches the feeling. The danger is an unnoticed turn and descent. The fix is to put the eyes on the attitude indicator, fly the instruments, and let the false sensation fade.
dup: What causes the leans and what wrong input does it invite?

concept: Coriolis illusion - caused by a turn held long enough for the fluid in the ear canal to move at the same speed as the canal, then a head movement on another axis
q: What causes the Coriolis illusion?
a: Being in a turn long enough for the fluid in the ear canal to move at the same speed as the canal, after which the canals report no turn at all. If the pilot then moves the head on a different axis, looking down at a chart or up at a switch, the settled fluid is abruptly disturbed and the brain reads a violent turn or acceleration about an entirely different axis.
dup: What is the Coriolis illusion and why is it so incapacitating?

concept: Coriolis illusion - the disoriented pilot may maneuver the aircraft into a dangerous attitude correcting a perceived attitude
q: Why is the Coriolis illusion so dangerous?
a: Because the sensation of tumbling about another axis is overwhelming, and the disoriented pilot may maneuver the aircraft into a dangerous attitude while trying to correct an attitude that does not exist. It is considered one of the most incapacitating illusions there is. Avoid it by not making sudden or extreme head movements during prolonged turns, especially at night or in instrument conditions.
dup: What is the Coriolis illusion and why is it so incapacitating?

concept: Graveyard spiral - occurs in a prolonged coordinated constant-rate turn as the fluid in the ear settles and the pilot forgets the turn
q: What is the graveyard spiral and how does it start?
a: It starts in a prolonged coordinated, constant-rate turn. The fluid in the inner ear settles, the canals stop reporting rotation, and the pilot forgets the airplane is turning. Because the turn is coordinated there is no slip or skid to feel, and in cloud or on a dark night there is nothing outside to contradict the false sensation of wings level.
dup: What is the graveyard spiral and how does it kill?

concept: Graveyard spiral - on recovery the pilot senses a turn in the opposite direction, returns to the original turn and loses altitude
q: How does the graveyard spiral kill a pilot?
a: When the disoriented pilot rolls level, the sensation is of turning in the opposite direction, so the pilot returns the airplane to its original turn and loses altitude in the process. Noticing the descent, the pilot pulls back and adds power, which only tightens the spiral and increases the rate of descent, down to the ground or to structural failure. Recover by leveling the wings on the attitude indicator first, then the pitch.
dup: What is the graveyard spiral and how does it kill?

concept: Somatogravic illusion - a rapid acceleration such as takeoff creates the illusion of a nose-up attitude
q: What is the somatogravic illusion?
a: A rapid acceleration, such as the acceleration experienced during takeoff, drives the otolith organs backward and creates a powerful illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. A rapid deceleration gives the reverse, a sensation of pitching down. It is strongest when there is no usable outside reference, which makes it a night and instrument departure problem.
dup: What is the somatogravic illusion and why is a go-around so dangerous?

concept: Somatogravic illusion - the disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low or dive attitude
q: What wrong input does the somatogravic illusion invite, and when is it most lethal?
a: The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low or dive attitude to correct a climb that is not happening. It is most lethal immediately after a night or low visibility takeoff and during a go-around, when the acceleration is greatest and there is least height to lose. The defense is to set a known pitch attitude and power on the instruments and fly them, ignoring the sensation.
dup: What is the somatogravic illusion and why is a go-around so dangerous?

concept: Inversion illusion - an abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level creates the illusion of tumbling backward
q: What is the inversion illusion?
a: An abrupt change from a climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of tumbling backward. The sudden reduction in the climb angle overstimulates the otolith organs, and the brain reads the change as going over backward even though the airplane has simply leveled off.
dup: What is the inversion illusion and what does it make a pilot do?

concept: Inversion illusion - the disoriented pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude, intensifying the illusion
q: What does the inversion illusion make a pilot do?
a: The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft abruptly into a nose-low attitude, which intensifies the illusion and can start a descent that is hard to recognize. The remedy is to level off smoothly rather than abruptly, especially at the top of a climb at night or in cloud, and to fly the attitude indicator rather than the sensation.
dup: What is the inversion illusion and what does it make a pilot do?

concept: Elevator illusion - an abrupt upward vertical acceleration, as in an updraft, creates the illusion of being in a climb
q: What is the elevator illusion?
a: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, such as occurs in an updraft, stimulates the otolith organs and creates the illusion of being in a climb. A downdraft produces the opposite sensation, of descending. It turns up in turbulence near thermals, over ridges and around convective cloud.
dup: What is the elevator illusion?

concept: Elevator illusion - the disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low attitude
q: What is the wrong reaction to the elevator illusion?
a: The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low attitude to stop a climb that the instruments do not show, which in a downdraft or near terrain can be fatal. Cross-check the altimeter, the vertical speed indicator and the attitude indicator, and make any correction from them rather than from the feeling of rising or sinking.
dup: What is the elevator illusion?

concept: False horizon - caused by a sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, an aurora borealis, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, or certain geometric patterns
q: What conditions produce the false horizon illusion?
a: Trying to align the aircraft with something that is not the true horizon: a sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, an aurora borealis, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars that blend into one another, or certain geometric ground patterns such as a lighted road or a shoreline. All of them are false references, and all are night or reduced visibility traps.
dup: What is the false horizon illusion?

concept: False horizon - the disoriented pilot may place the aircraft in a dangerous attitude
q: What does the false horizon illusion make a pilot do?
a: The disoriented pilot may place the aircraft in a dangerous attitude, banking or pitching to line the wings up with the false reference while the real horizon lies somewhere else. The defense is to treat the attitude indicator as the horizon whenever the natural horizon is dim, sloping or ambiguous, and to back it up with heading, altitude and the turn coordinator.

concept: Autokinesis - in the dark a stationary light stared at for a prolonged period appears to move
q: What is autokinesis?
a: When flying in the dark, a stationary light may appear to move if it is stared at for a prolonged period of time. With no surrounding visual reference, the small involuntary movements of the eye are interpreted by the brain as movement of the light itself, and it can begin after only a few seconds of fixation.
dup: What is autokinesis and how do you defeat it?

concept: Autokinesis - the disoriented pilot may align the aircraft with the perceived moving light and lose control
q: Why does autokinesis matter, and how do you defeat it?
a: The disoriented pilot may attempt to align the aircraft with the perceived moving light and lose control of the aircraft, or may take a star or a ground light for traffic and maneuver against it. Defeat it by not staring: keep the eyes moving with a normal scan, look at any single light for only a few seconds, and check it against the flight instruments and other outside references.

concept: 91.17 - blood alcohol level must be less than .04 percent
q: What blood alcohol concentration does 91.17 allow for acting as a crewmember?
a: Your blood alcohol concentration must be less than 0.04 percent by weight; at 0.04 percent or more you may not act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft, and you may not do so while under the influence of alcohol at any reading. In plain terms it is the sober crew rule, and it lives in 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A (General), section 91.17 Alcohol or drugs.
dup: What are the exact alcohol limits for acting as a required crewmember?

concept: 91.17 - 8 hours must pass between drinking alcohol and piloting an aircraft, 8 hours bottle to throttle
q: How long must you wait between drinking and flying?
a: 8 hours must pass between consuming any alcoholic beverage and acting or attempting to act as a crewmember, the familiar eight hours bottle to throttle. The same rule bars flying while under the influence or while using any drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety, and it requires you to submit to a test when a law enforcement officer asks. 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A (General), section 91.17 Alcohol or drugs.
dup: What are the exact alcohol limits for acting as a required crewmember?

concept: As little as one ounce of alcohol decreases the speed and strength of muscular reflexes, lessens the efficiency of eye movements while reading, and increases the frequency of errors
q: What does even a small amount of alcohol do to a pilot?
a: Alcohol can greatly impair the efficiency of the human body, and as little as one ounce can decrease the speed and strength of muscular reflexes, lessen the efficiency of eye movements while reading, and increase the frequency at which errors are committed. Judgment goes first and the pilot does not notice it going, and altitude magnifies everything because alcohol also produces histotoxic hypoxia.
dup: Is being legal on the 8-hour and 0.04 percent rule the same as being fit to fly?

concept: The body requires about 3 hours to rid itself of all the alcohol in one mixed drink or one beer
q: How long does the body take to clear one drink, and what does that mean for the 8-hour rule?
a: About 3 hours to rid itself of all the alcohol contained in one mixed drink or one beer, and nothing speeds that up; coffee, oxygen, food and a cold shower do not. Several drinks can therefore leave measurable alcohol and a hangover well past the eight hour minimum, so meeting 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A (General), section 91.17 Alcohol or drugs is not the same thing as being fit to fly.

concept: Definition of night - the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, per the Air Almanac, converted to local time
q: How is night defined?
a: Night is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time. The definition is in 14 CFR Part 1, Definitions and Abbreviations, which has no subparts, section 1.1 General definitions, and it is the period in which night flight time is logged. Two other night periods, one for lights and one for passenger currency, are defined differently.
dup: How is night defined for the purpose of logging night flight time?

concept: Definition of civil twilight - morning begins at 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise; evening begins at sunset and ends at 6 degrees below; usually 20 to 35 minutes
q: Define morning and evening civil twilight.
a: Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise. Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun reaches 6 degrees below the horizon. It usually lasts between 20 and 35 minutes, longer at high latitudes and in winter, and the times are published in the Air Almanac for your location.

concept: Definition of sunset - the upper edge of the sun, the upper limb, sinks just under the horizon
q: What exactly is sunset?
a: Sunset occurs when the upper limb of the sun, that is its upper edge, sinks just under the horizon. It is not the moment the sun's center crosses, and it is not when the sky goes dark. Sunset is the instant evening civil twilight begins, and it is the instant your position and anticollision lights must be on.

concept: Definition of sunrise - the upper limb rises just above the horizon
q: What exactly is sunrise?
a: Sunrise occurs when the upper limb of the sun, that is its upper edge, rises just above the horizon. It marks the end of morning civil twilight, and it is the moment at which the position lights and anticollision lights may be turned off.

concept: The three night periods compared - lights, logging night, and night landing currency, and how they nest between sunset and sunrise
q: Draw me the three night periods between sunset and sunrise. Which is widest, which narrowest?
a: Widest is the lights period, sunset to sunrise. Inside it sits night itself for logging, from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight. Narrowest is the night landing currency period, from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. So the evening order is sunset, then the end of civil twilight some 20 to 35 minutes later, then the currency clock at 1 hour after sunset; in the morning the order reverses.
dup: What are the three different definitions of night a commercial pilot must keep straight?

concept: Diagram - position lights and anticollision lights must be turned ON at sunset and may be turned OFF at sunrise
q: Between which two events must your position and anticollision lights be on?
a: From sunset to sunrise: they must be turned on at sunset and may be turned off at sunrise. This is the widest of the three night periods, starting before night legally begins and ending after it ends, so the lights are burning through both civil twilights while the logbook still says day. 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C (Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements), section 91.209 Aircraft lights.
dup: What period governs when position lights must be on?

concept: Diagram - night begins and logging of night hours begins at the end of evening civil twilight, and ends at the beginning of morning civil twilight
q: On the night diagram, where exactly does logging of night time start and stop?
a: Logging starts at the end of evening civil twilight, roughly 20 to 35 minutes after sunset, and stops at the beginning of morning civil twilight, roughly 20 to 35 minutes before sunrise. Time flown between sunset and the end of civil twilight is day time in the logbook even though the lights must already be on, and the same applies at the other end of the night.

concept: Diagram - night landing currency starts 1 hour after sunset and ends 1 hour before sunrise, inside the night period
q: When does the night landing currency window open and close relative to sunset and sunrise?
a: It opens 1 hour after sunset and closes 1 hour before sunrise, so it sits inside the period that counts as night for logging and well inside the lights period. Landings made between the end of evening civil twilight and 1 hour after sunset may be logged as night landings but do not count toward night passenger currency. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).

concept: 61.57(b) - no person may act as PIC carrying passengers from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise unless the requirements were met within the preceding 90 days
q: State the night takeoff and landing experience requirement.
a: No person may act as pilot in command carrying passengers during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise unless, within the preceding 90 days, that person made at least 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in that same period, as sole manipulator of the controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and type if a type rating is required. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).

concept: 61.57(b) applies only to carrying passengers - a pilot who is not night current may still fly at night solo
q: Your night currency has lapsed. May you still fly at night?
a: Yes, but not with passengers between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise. You may fly alone at night, and you may carry passengers between sunset and 1 hour after sunset, so you can go out solo and regain currency with 3 takeoffs and 3 full stop landings inside the window. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).

concept: 61.57(b) - at least 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop, made within that same period, in the preceding 90 days
q: How many takeoffs and landings, of what kind, in what period, for night currency?
a: At least 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days, and each one must have been flown during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. Touch and go landings never count at night, unlike the daytime passenger rule, where full stop landings are required only in a tailwheel airplane. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).
dup: When must the three takeoffs and landings be to a full stop?

concept: 61.57(b) - the person must have acted as sole manipulator of the flight controls
q: Can the takeoffs and landings for night currency be flown with an instructor on the controls?
a: No. You must have been the sole manipulator of the flight controls for each of the 3 takeoffs and 3 full stop landings. An instructor may be aboard, and may even be the pilot in command, but you have to fly them yourself for them to count. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).

concept: 61.57(b) - in an aircraft of the same category, class and type
q: In what aircraft must your night takeoffs and landings have been flown?
a: In an aircraft of the same category, class and type, where a type rating is required. Category is the broad grouping, such as airplane; class is single-engine land, multi-engine land, single-engine sea or multi-engine sea; type is the specific make and model when a type rating applies. Night landings in your PA-28-161 keep you current for any airplane single-engine land. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b).

concept: Logging night flying - loggable any time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, and the airplane must be night VFR equipped
q: When may you log night flight time, and what must the airplane have aboard?
a: Any time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight. The airplane must be equipped for night VFR under 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C (Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements), section 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, paragraph (c), and you record the conditions of flight under Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.51 Pilot logbooks.

concept: 91.209 - from sunset to sunrise position lights and anticollision lights, if installed, are required to be turned on
q: What does 91.209 require of your lights, and when may the anticollision lights be off?
a: From sunset to sunrise no person may operate an aircraft unless it has lighted position lights, and an aircraft equipped with an anticollision light system must have those lights lighted. In plain terms, lights on at sunset and off at sunrise. The anticollision lights may be switched off when the pilot in command decides that, because of operating conditions, it is in the interest of safety to do so. 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C (Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements), section 91.209 Aircraft lights.

concept: Definition of a stall - a rapid decrease in lift caused by separation of airflow from the wing's surface brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack
q: Define a stall.
a: A stall is a rapid decrease in lift caused by the separation of airflow from the wing's surface, brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack. The boundary layer detaches, the smooth flow over the upper surface breaks up, lift falls off sharply while drag rises, the center of pressure moves aft, and the nose usually drops.
dup: What happens to lift in a stall?

concept: A stall can occur at any pitch attitude or airspeed
q: At what airspeed and in what attitude does a wing stall?
a: A wing stalls at the critical angle of attack, not at any particular airspeed, so a stall can occur at any pitch attitude and at any airspeed. The published stall speed applies only at one weight in wings-level, unaccelerated, one G flight; add bank, load factor or an abrupt pull and the airplane will stall at a higher speed, even nose-low and fast.
dup: Does an aircraft stall at a particular airspeed or a particular angle of attack?

concept: Three flight situations in which the critical angle of attack is most commonly exceeded: low speed, high speed and turning flight
q: In which three flight situations is the critical angle of attack most commonly exceeded?
a: Low speed, high speed and turning flight. In each of them the pilot asks the wing for more lift than it can give at that angle of attack: slowing until the angle needed to hold altitude reaches the critical angle; pulling abruptly while fast; or loading the wing in a bank. Knowing all three stops a pilot from assuming the airplane is safe merely because the airspeed is high.

concept: Low speed stall - as airspeed decreases the angle of attack must increase to hold altitude until the wing can no longer support the aircraft
q: Explain the low speed stall.
a: As airspeed decreases, the angle of attack must be increased to retain the lift required to maintain altitude. Eventually an angle of attack is reached at which the wing is not producing enough lift to support the aircraft, and it stalls. This is the classic straight-ahead power-off stall, and it is the case the published stall speed in the handbook describes.

concept: High speed stall - the critical angle of attack can be reached at any speed through an abrupt change in angle of attack
q: How can an airplane stall at high speed?
a: The critical angle of attack can be reached at any speed. With an abrupt change in angle of attack, such as a sharp pull during a pull-up or a dive recovery, the critical angle can be exceeded while the airspeed indicator still reads well into the green arc. This is the accelerated stall, and it tends to be sudden and sharp, often with a wing dropping.
dup: How does load factor affect stall speed?

concept: Turning stall - centrifugal force adds to weight, the wing must produce extra lift, and angle of attack must increase as bank increases
q: Why is the wing closer to a stall in a turn?
a: In a turn, centrifugal force is added to the aircraft's weight and the wing must produce sufficient additional lift to counterbalance the combined load. Since the angle of attack must be increased as bank increases, the margin to the critical angle shrinks with bank, and stall speed rises with load factor: a level 60 degree bank gives 2 G and raises stall speed about 41 percent. Near the ground that margin is everything.

concept: Static stability - the initial tendency, or direction of movement, back to equilibrium
q: What is static stability?
a: Static stability is the initial tendency, the direction of movement, that an aircraft displays toward or away from its original state of equilibrium immediately after it is disturbed. It describes only that first reaction in the first instant; it says nothing about what the motion does afterward, which is the job of dynamic stability.

concept: Positive static stability - the initial tendency to return to the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed
q: What is positive static stability?
a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to return to its original state of equilibrium after being disturbed. Displace the nose with a bump and the airplane starts straight back toward the trimmed attitude on its own. Airplanes certificated in the normal category are required to show it about all three axes within the normal operating envelope.

concept: Neutral static stability - the initial tendency to remain in the new condition after equilibrium has been disturbed
q: What is neutral static stability?
a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to remain in the new condition after its equilibrium has been disturbed. It neither moves back toward the original state nor further away from it, but simply stays where the disturbance left it. A ball resting on a flat tabletop is the usual picture.

concept: Negative static stability - the initial tendency to continue away from the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed
q: What is negative static stability?
a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to continue away from the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed, so the displacement grows from the first instant. It is static instability, and the usual picture is a ball balanced on top of a dome, which rolls away once nudged. Loading the center of gravity aft of the limit moves an airplane in this direction.

concept: Dynamic stability - the behavior over time after being disturbed from the trimmed condition
q: What is dynamic stability?
a: Dynamic stability describes the motion an aircraft displays over time after being disturbed from its trimmed condition, in other words what happens to the oscillation once the initial tendency has acted. The two forms are independent: an airplane can be positively statically stable and still have negative dynamic stability, giving oscillations that grow with each cycle.

concept: Positive dynamic stability - over time the motion decreases in amplitude and the object returns toward equilibrium
q: What is positive dynamic stability?
a: Over time the motion of the displaced object decreases in amplitude and the object returns toward the equilibrium state, each oscillation smaller than the one before it until the motion dies out. A trimmed airplane whose phugoid damps out over a few cycles after a disturbance is showing it, and it is what makes an airplane restful to fly hands off.

concept: Neutral dynamic stability - once displaced the motion neither decreases nor increases in amplitude; a worn automobile shock absorber
q: What is neutral dynamic stability?
a: Once displaced, the object neither decreases nor increases in amplitude, so the oscillation simply continues at the same size indefinitely. A worn automobile shock absorber exhibits this tendency: the car keeps bouncing after a bump instead of the motion dying away.

concept: Negative dynamic stability - over time the motion increases and becomes more divergent
q: What is negative dynamic stability?
a: Over time the motion of the displaced object increases in amplitude and becomes more divergent, each oscillation larger than the last, until the pilot intervenes or the structure is overstressed. It is dynamic instability, and it is not acceptable in a certificated airplane in any mode the pilot is expected to control.
